contribution: The first unit of the French chapter: complete beginners learn the phrases of a first meeting (greetings, name, origin, home, languages, goodbye), choose between tu and vous and between Bonjour, Bonsoir and Salut, practise four pronunciation points for Finnish speakers, and use them in a role-play set at a scenario visit to ITER.
learn: greet people in French, choosing between *Bonjour*, *Bonsoir* and *Salut* and between *tu* and *vous*.
introduce yourself: your name, where you come from and live, and which languages you speak.
pronounce silent final letters, the French *r*, nasal vowels and the liaison in *vous êtes* understandably.

activities.text: ITER is in the commune of Saint-Paul-lez-Durance (Bouches-du-Rhône), about 35 kilometres north of Aix-en-Provence. Its seven members are China, the European Union, India, Japan, Korea, Russia and the United States, so many people at work speak English, but the region around the site speaks French. You step off the bus at the ITER visitor centre. It is ten o'clock in the morning and already warm. A woman with a visitor badge on her jacket smiles at you and says « Bonjour ! » Your teacher is still on the bus.
activities.question: What do you say back, and what do you say next?

activities.title: Think about it: greetings and the French you know
activities.prompt: In Finnish, you might say *moi* to a friend, *hei* to a teacher and *hyvää päivää* to an older stranger. Who do you greet with which word, and why? Then write down every French word or phrase you already know or recognise, for example from films, songs, food or signs.
activities.pair: Discuss with a partner for two minutes, then write a few lines together.
activities.model: We choose the greeting by the person and the situation: friends get *moi* or *terve*, adults we do not know get *hei* or *päivää*, and very formal situations *hyvää päivää*. French works the same way, but the polite form is used more. French we already recognise: bonjour, merci, au revoir, oui, non, s'il vous plaît, croissant, café, restaurant, bon appétit.
criteria: I name at least two greetings and say who each one is for.
I explain that the choice depends on how well we know the person and how formal the situation is.
I list some French words or phrases I already know.

activities.title: Prediction 1: the first word
activities.prompt: It is Monday, ten o'clock in the morning. You arrive at the reception desk of the visitor centre. The receptionist is a woman of about fifty whom you have never met. What do you say first?

choices.feedback: Yes. Bonjour is the daytime greeting for anyone, and madame makes it polite. An adult you have never met, at work: this is exactly the place for the polite form.
Salut means *hi*, and it is for friends and people your own age. To a receptionist you do not know it sounds too familiar, as if you said *moikka* to a stranger at an office. Use Bonjour, madame.
Bonsoir is polite, but it means *good evening*. At ten in the morning the greeting is Bonjour.
Au revoir means *goodbye*: you say it when you leave. When you arrive, say Bonjour, madame.

activities.title: Prediction 2: asking a name
activities.prompt: An engineer of about forty shows your group around. You want to ask her name. Which question fits best? You will find out in the theory summary.

choices.feedback: Right. She is an adult you have just met, in a work situation, so you use *vous*: Comment vous appelez-vous ? If she later says On peut se tutoyer, you can change to *tu*.
This is correct French, but it uses *tu*, the informal *you*. To an adult you have just met at work it sounds too familiar. Use *vous* until she offers *tu*: Comment vous appelez-vous ?
Je m'appelle … means *my name is …*: it is the answer, not the question. To ask, say Comment vous appelez-vous ?
This is polite, but it asks *where do you live?* To ask her name, say Comment vous appelez-vous ?

activities.title: Listen: the phrases of a first meeting
activities.text: Listen to each phrase, first slowly, then at normal speed, and repeat it aloud. Read the tip: it tells you which letters are silent or how a sound is made.

activities.title: A first meeting at ITER
activities.text: Read the dialogue first and notice three things: which greeting each person uses, whether they say *tu* or *vous*, and in which order the topics come.

activities.title: Order an evening conversation
What did you notice?
activities.prompt: Compare the two conversations: Aino and Claire at the visitor centre, and Eetu and Léa at the hotel. Why do Eetu and Léa say *tu* and *Salut*, while Aino and Claire say *vous* and *Bonjour*?

choices.text: Eetu and Léa are young people of the same age, while Claire is an adult Aino has just met at work.
choices.feedback: Yes. The choice depends on the people and the situation: young people of the same age use *tu* at once; with an adult in a formal or work setting you use *vous*.

choices.text: Because it is evening: *tu* and *Salut* are used in the evening.
choices.feedback: The time of day changes only Bonjour to Bonsoir. *Tu* or *vous* depends on the people, not on the clock: Eetu would say *vous* to the hotel receptionist in the evening too.

choices.text: Because Léa lives in Marseille, and people in the south always say *tu*.
choices.feedback: Where someone lives does not decide it. In every part of France you say *vous* to an adult you do not know, and young people of the same age say *tu* to each other.

choices.text: Because Eetu speaks only a little French, and *tu* is easier for beginners.
choices.feedback: *Tu* is not a beginner's form: it is the informal *you*. Aino speaks only a little French too, but she correctly uses *vous* with an adult she has just met.

activities.title: Complete the sentences
What does it mean?
Role-play: meeting at ITER
activities.text:
Work in pairs. **Round 1:** A is a Finnish student, B is a researcher at ITER who speaks French (choose where B comes from: France, Italy, Japan, India …). Meet at the visitor centre in the morning, introduce yourselves and say goodbye. **Round 2:** swap roles. Now you are two young visitors who meet at the hotel in the evening. Speak without reading if you can; the word bank is there if you get stuck.

Word bank

Bonjour, madame / monsieur, Salut, Bonsoir, Je m'appelle …, Comment vous appelez-vous ?, Comment tu t'appelles ?, Enchanté(e), Je viens de Finlande, Je suis finlandais / finlandaise, J'habite à …, Je parle un peu français, Parlez-vous anglais ?, Merci beaucoup, Au revoir, À bientôt

Sentence starters

  • Bonjour, madame. Je m'appelle …
  • Je viens de … J'habite à …
  • Et vous, d'où venez-vous ?
  • Pardon, je parle un peu français. Parlez-vous anglais ?
  • Merci beaucoup ! Au revoir et à bientôt !

activities.title: Role-play: your dialogue
activities.prompt: After both rounds, write the French of the dialogue you performed in round 1, or at least six lines of it.
activities.pair: Perform the role-play with a partner first, then write it together. If you can, perform it to another pair, who check it with the criteria below.
activities.model: **Round 1 (polite):** - B: Bonjour ! Bienvenue à ITER. - A: Bonjour, monsieur. Je m'appelle Eetu. Comment vous appelez-vous ? - B: Je m'appelle Marco. Je suis italien. Enchanté ! D'où venez-vous ? - A: Je viens de Finlande. Je suis finlandais. J'habite à Espoo. - B: Comment ça va ? - A: Ça va bien, merci. Et vous ? - B: Très bien, merci. - A: Je parle un peu français. Parlez-vous anglais ? - B: Oui, bien sûr ! - A: Merci beaucoup, monsieur. Au revoir ! - B: Au revoir, Eetu. À bientôt ! **Round 2 (informal, in the evening):** - A: Salut ! Je m'appelle Léa. Et toi, comment tu t'appelles ? - B: Salut ! Je m'appelle Aino. Je viens de Finlande. - A: Où habites-tu ? - B: J'habite à Espoo. Et toi ? - A: J'habite à Marseille. Bon, à bientôt, Aino ! - B: Salut, Léa ! À bientôt !
criteria: **Communicates the message:** we greet, say our names, where we come from and live, which languages we speak, and say goodbye.
**Polite form chosen correctly:** in round 1 we use *Bonjour, madame / monsieur* and *vous*; in round 2 *Salut* or *Bonsoir* and *tu*.
**Pronunciation understandable:** we do not pronounce the silent final letters, and we link *vous‿êtes* / *vous‿appelez*.
We speak mostly from memory and keep the conversation going when we get stuck (*Pardon ?*, *Encore une fois, s'il vous plaît*).

activities.title: Extension: introducing a classmate
activities.text:
To introduce someone else, change *je* to **il** (he) or **elle** (she). For a woman or a girl, the nationality takes *-e*, as before. Start with Voici … (This is …).
Now introduce your partner from the role-play to another pair: Voici … Il / Elle s'appelle … Il / Elle vient de … Il / Elle habite à …

activities.title: 1. Greeting a professor
activities.prompt: At nine in the morning you enter a seminar room at ITER. Professor Dubois, a senior physicist you have never met, is standing at the door. What do you say?

choices.feedback: Salut is the informal *hi* for friends and people your age. To a professor you have never met it sounds disrespectful. Say Bonjour, monsieur.
Yes: the daytime greeting, made polite with *monsieur*. The professor may offer a less formal tone later; it is his choice, not yours.
The tone is polite, but Bonsoir means *good evening*. At nine in the morning, say Bonjour, monsieur.
Both Salut and *tu* are informal: this is how you talk to a new friend of your age. To a professor: Bonjour, monsieur. Comment vous appelez-vous ?

activities.title: 2. Saying your nationality
activities.prompt: Aino, a Finnish girl, wants to say *I am Finnish*. Which sentence is correct?

choices.feedback: This is the form for a boy or a man. A girl or a woman adds *-e*: Je suis finlandaise. You can hear the difference: the *s* is silent in *finlandais* but sounds like *z* in *finlandaise*.
Finlande is the country. With *je suis* you need the nationality: Je suis finlandaise. The country goes with *venir de*: Je viens de Finlande.
Yes. *Finlandaise* is the feminine form, and in French a nationality is written with a small letter.
*Je viens* means *I come*, and it needs *de* and the country: Je viens de Finlande. For the nationality, use *je suis*: Je suis finlandaise.

activities.title: 3. Pronouncing vous êtes
activities.prompt: How do you pronounce vous êtes (you are)?

choices.text: *vu-ZET*: the *s* of *vous* sounds like a *z* and starts the next word.
choices.feedback: Yes. This is a liaison: the silent *s* of *vous* is heard because *êtes* starts with a vowel, and in liaison an *s* sounds like *z*. After *vous* before a verb it is always made.

choices.text: *vu ET*, with a short pause and no consonant between the words.
choices.feedback: People will understand you, but it sounds wrong: the liaison after *vous* before a verb is compulsory. Link the words: *vu-ZET*.

choices.text: *vus E-tes*, saying every letter as in Finnish.
choices.feedback: This is the Finnish habit of saying every letter. The final *-es* of *êtes* is silent, and the *s* of *vous* sounds like *z* when it is linked: *vu-ZET*.

choices.text: *vu-SET*, with a sharp *s* as in *sauna*.
choices.feedback: You made the liaison, well done, but in liaison the *s* is voiced: it sounds like *z*, as in English *zoo*. Say *vu-ZET*.

activities.title: 4. Write: introduce yourself
activities.prompt: Before the (imagined) visit, your teacher asks each student to write a short French introduction for the researchers you will meet. Write four or five sentences: a greeting, your name, where you come from and live, your nationality, which languages you speak, and a polite ending.
activities.model: Bonjour ! Je m'appelle Eetu. Je viens de Finlande et j'habite à Espoo. Je suis finlandais. Je parle finnois, suédois et anglais, et je parle un peu français. Merci et à bientôt !
criteria: I greet politely (*Bonjour*, not *Salut*: I am writing to adults I do not know).
I say my name with *Je m'appelle …*, my country with *Je viens de …* and my town with *J'habite à …*.
I use the right form of the nationality: *finlandais* for a boy or man, *finlandaise* for a girl or woman.
I say which languages I speak and end politely (*Merci*, *À bientôt*, *Au revoir*).
